surface_forms: un aventurier du nom de Swann

appraisal_events.evidence: "Aussi y eut-il un mouvement de curiosité et de déférence quand il entra. C'était Morel," his moral testimony having led to a conviction, while the narrator alone knows he had been kept by M. de Charlus and by Saint-Loup.
appraisal_events.explanation: Society greets Morel with public curiosity and deference on the strength of a moral authority the narrator privately knows to be unfounded, so the elevation is real within the scene but undercut for the reader.

appraisal_events.evidence: After a clean break with his old milieu, Bloch makes "une apparition de grand homme" in the reconstituted society, taken by the young and by fashionable women for a kind of genius, though the narrator privately calls his books unoriginal and sophistical.
appraisal_events.explanation: The new, forgetful society elevates Bloch to the status of a man of talent who seems always to have belonged there, an elevation the narrator's own judgment quietly contradicts.

appraisal_events.evidence: Asked about Gilberte's mother, a young aristocrat says she first married "un aventurier du nom de Swann" and later one of society's most prominent men, the comte de Forcheville — a claim the narrator calls "monstrueuse," and which duchesses who had actually been Swann's intimate friends would never have recognized.
appraisal_events.explanation: Generational forgetting inverts the two men's real standing, recasting Swann as a disreputable adventurer and elevating Forcheville in his place; the narrator explicitly marks this reordering as false even as it stands uncontested among the new arrivals.

status_effects.explanation: His entrance is met with visible curiosity and deference from those present, a witnessed rise in standing on the strength of his courtroom testimony.
Bloch is now regarded by the young and by society women as a man of rare talent, even genius, a clear local rise in reputation.

Among the new generation he is locally recast as a mere adventurer, a diminishment the narrator regards as false but which nonetheless stands as the passage's demonstrated social reality for these speakers.
In the same erroneous account he is named one of the most prominent men in society, a local (if narrator-contested) elevation relative to Swann.

ambiguities: The reversal of Swann's and Forcheville's reputations is presented through an ignorant young aristocrat and is explicitly rejected by the narrator as monstrous, so its status movement reflects a contested local social belief rather than a narrator-endorsed verdict.
